children: The revival of crude exports from the Persian Gulf is starting to weigh on the physical market, as Middle East oil metrics indicate near-term supply is outpacing demand for the first time since July, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

The nearest timespread for the regional Dubai benchmark was in a bearish contango structure at the start of the week, with the November contract at a discount of ~$2/bbl to December, traders and brokers told Bloomberg.

The Middle East's Arab oil-producing nations reportedly are shipping crude at about the same rate as before the war started in February, while Iranian exports remain effectively halted; combined exports from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, and Kuwait rose 10% to more than 15M bbl/day last month.
Elsewhere, North Sea oil cargoes—which help set the price of the world's most important physical oil benchmark, Dated Brent—have also declined in recent days, according to the report.
The increased supply, as well as the possibility of renewed talks to pursue a peace deal between the U.S. and Iran, has helped cool global oil prices after they hit a six-month high in October.

Oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz is keeping the market well supplied, and "oil that is actually loaded and shipped is getting cheaper relative to benchmarks—a sign of rising supply, not just nervous futures traders," Phil Flynn of Price Futures Group said in a note.

Crude oil futures fell modestly Tuesday in a session that saw prices rise before pulling back, as traders weighed reports of U.S. strikes on Iranian targets against continued signs of progress toward a diplomatic agreement between the two countries.

Reports of back-channel discussions between the U.S. and Iran, along with statements from President Trump and Vice President Vance hinting at progress toward a possible agreement, had helped drive crude futures down more than 7% on Monday.
Oil has weakened because of U.S.-Iran diplomacy, but there is still little evidence of an actual breakthrough, Amarpreet Singh of Barclays said in a note.

"On the surface, there is little change in the Iranian position, but it is difficult to tell how much of that is just posturing," although indications of some flexibility have "swung market participants back into the hopeful camp," Singh wrote.

"The market wants to believe we're going to get a peace deal, but I think a peace deal is basically part of the Trump administration's effort to paint a rosy picture with the unpopular war effort on election day," Mizuho commodity specialist Robert Yawger said in a note.
